findings.reason: The protected source presents an expert-quality shortest-path solution: monotonic segment scans precompute every roll endpoint, four direct transitions expose the maze graph, and tuple-keyed Dijkstra resolves both distance and lexicographic objectives. The implementation is clear, conventional, and materially preferable to no inert alternative, so no candidate is justified.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode problem 499 and its Python maze/ball/hole string contract. Each transition commits to a wall-bounded roll but truncates it at an intervening hole, traveled distance excludes the current cell, and the heap's path key implements the required complete-string tie break.

The immutable native source is bound to verified submission 2065123405. It and the protected app source have the same horizontal and vertical segment preprocessing, endpoint tables, target interruption checks, distance calculation, heap tuple order, best-pair relaxation, stale-entry rejection, success return, and failure return; only the native class and type wrapper differ.

The three disconnected-hole workloads contain 16, 64, and 256 cells, span 16x, and require exhaustion of reachable states after endpoint preprocessing. The protected source passed all 10 correctness cases and all three performance tiers, including the legal 100 by 100 boundary. A correct Bellman-Ford control passed every output but failed only the runtime verdict with relative growth exponent +0.27.

The current-targeted Approach exactly derives maximal open segments, constant-structure endpoint transitions, hole interruption, weighted relaxation, tuple-keyed lexicographic ordering, stale-entry rejection, and first-current-hole termination. It distinguishes structural graph costs from the explicit worst-case time and space needed to construct, retain, and compare immutable path strings.

The hash-bound modular Reference was checked directly against the authenticated Premium statement. It preserves rolling and hole semantics, direction instructions, distance and lexicographic rules, all three examples and the first two explanations, all ten displayed constraints, and source section order. Both source images were independently recreated as accessible tables with the same maze, ball, hole, and wall relationships.

coverage: All three authenticated Premium source examples now appear first and in source order with their exact mazes, ball and hole coordinates, and route strings. The missing four-by-seven example and its dldr result were restored.
The contract-invalid same-cell fixture was removed, the invented open-square example was relabelled as a trial, and both formerly hidden correctness cases are now visible trials.

Boundaries cover 1 by 2 and 2 by 1 minimum mazes, a legal 100 by 100 maximum maze, coordinates 0 and 99, distinct in-bounds empty positions, walls and open cells, horizontal and vertical rolls, and maximum path distance.

Material semantics cover a hole interrupting a roll before the wall, an unreachable hole, forced turns, equal-distance lexicographic selection, and the distinction between traveled distance and instruction count.

An independent step-by-step rolling Dijkstra oracle verified all ten correctness cases and all three benchmark outputs, 10,228 exhaustive legal small-maze routes, and 1,000 randomized routes. The protected implementation agreed throughout.
All ten correctness cases are visible samples or trials; the unchanged 16-, 64-, and 256-cell disconnected-hole workloads remain hidden and performance-only in benchmark.json.
